title: CI: fix `check_storage_layout` for new contracts
body:
There's the [core-contracts-storage-check](https://github.com/ubiquity/ubiquity-dollar/blob/20799bedf5ee4d40d2863653f7bc2fe68a2ce3fa/.github/workflows/core-contracts-storage-check.yml) workflow which checks that contracts' storage is not messed on contract upgrades.

Check these CI runs which fails with the `No workflow run found with an artifact named...` error:
- https://github.com/ubiquity/ubiquity-dollar/actions/runs/11125075713/job/30912062971?pr=959
- https://github.com/ubiquity/ubiquity-dollar/actions/runs/11145695030/job/30975996318?pr=971

The issue is that when a **new contract** is added the [core-contracts-storage-check](https://github.com/ubiquity/ubiquity-dollar/blob/20799bedf5ee4d40d2863653f7bc2fe68a2ce3fa/.github/workflows/core-contracts-storage-check.yml) starts to fail while the expected behavior for the CI workflow to pass because we don't need to check storage layout for newly added contracts (because storage of the newly added contract hasn't been updated hence storage collision could not occur).

So as a part of this issue we should make sure that:
1. [core-contracts-storage-check](https://github.com/ubiquity/ubiquity-dollar/blob/20799bedf5ee4d40d2863653f7bc2fe68a2ce3fa/.github/workflows/core-contracts-storage-check.yml) is not failing for newly added contracts
2. [diamond-storage-check.yml](https://github.com/ubiquity/ubiquity-dollar/blob/20799bedf5ee4d40d2863653f7bc2fe68a2ce3fa/.github/workflows/diamond-storage-check.yml) is not failing for newly added libraries

P.S. Pls provide a QA in the related PR with these scenarios:
1) No storage updates, CI passing
2) Storage update, no collision, CI passing
3) Storage update, collision, CI failing
4) New contract added, CI passing

title: Integrate Liquity V1 Stability Pool for LUSD Collateral Yield
body:
## Problem
Plain LUSD collateral earns 0% yield. Integrate Stability Pool for ~6.28% APR ([Dune data](https://dune.com/liquity/liquity-v1)) to fund governance token buybacks, without disrupting liquidity.

## Solution
Add `StabilityPoolFacet` via diamond proxy. Auto-deposit LUSD to pool on mint; withdraw principal on redeem. Harvest ETH/LQTY yields during redeems for buybacks/compounding (protocol-owned only). Piggyback ops on user txs for gas efficiency.

## Alternatives Considered
- AAVE (~3.24% yield, more complex).
- Leverage/LPs (higher risk).
- V2 migration (future option for multi-collateral).

## Implementation Spec
### ~~Prerequisites~~
- ~~Audit facet (~$10-20K budget).~~
- ~~Integrate `IStabilityPool.sol` (address: 0x66017D22b0f8556afDd19e1e5b5f1cbD89a6C337).~~
- ~~Add 1inch/Uniswap for swaps.~~
- ~~New storage: `totalPrincipalInPool` (uint256), `protocolTreasury` (address).~~

### Facet Functions
- `depositToPool(uint256 amount)`: Call `provideToSP(amount, address(0))`.
- `withdrawFromPool(uint256 amount)`: Call `withdrawFromSP(amount)`.
- `harvestRewards()`: Claim rewards, swap (e.g., 50% to LUSD for compounding, 50% to governance token for buybacks).

### Flows
- **Mint**: Transfer LUSD → Deposit to pool → Mint uUSD → Update `totalPrincipalInPool += amount`.
- **Redeem**: Burn uUSD → Calc principal → Withdraw/transfer principal → Harvest if rewards > threshold (route to treasury) → Update `totalPrincipalInPool -= amount`.

### Over-Collateralization
Value pool as LUSD equivalent (Chainlink oracles for ETH/LQTY). Redemptions: principal only.

### Monitoring/Automation
- Chainlink/Gelato for optional harvests. It would be nice to sell the ETH/LQTY for LUSD and boost holdings as soon as it is rewarded by the stability pool.
- Dune alerts for APR/supply.

## Testing
- Unit: Deposit/withdraw/harvest (Foundry).
- Integration: Mainnet fork; simulate liquidations.
- Edges: Low liquidity, volatility, mass redeems. Gas: <200K extra per tx.

## Deployment
1. Deploy facet.
2. `diamondCut` via multisig.
3. Verify on Etherscan.
4. Phased: Opt-in for new deposits.

## ~~Risks/Mitigations~~
- ~~Yield variability: Fallback to plain LUSD if APR <3%.~~
- ~~Supply crunch: Auto-withdraw if < $10M.~~
- ~~Security: Audit for reentrancy.~~

title: Arbitrage bot
body:
In order to maintain [Dollar token](https://github.com/ubiquity/ubiquity-dollar/blob/0a230f977ad91bbfb01dd28bc1d2ea77faed5237/packages/contracts/src/dollar/core/UbiquityDollarToken.sol) USD peg [LibUbiquityPool](https://github.com/ubiquity/ubiquity-dollar/blob/0a230f977ad91bbfb01dd28bc1d2ea77faed5237/packages/contracts/src/dollar/libraries/LibUbiquityPool.sol) provides the following arbitrage mechanic:
1. If Dollar token USD price >1$ (on a secondary market) then arbitragers are incentivised to 
a) Mint 1 Dollar token for 1 USD of collateral in the [LibUbiquityPool](https://github.com/ubiquity/ubiquity-dollar/blob/0a230f977ad91bbfb01dd28bc1d2ea77faed5237/packages/contracts/src/dollar/libraries/LibUbiquityPool.sol)
b) Sell 1 Dollar token on a secondary market
2. On the contrary, If Dollar token USD price <1$ (on a secondary market) then arbitragers are incentivised to:
a) Buy cheap Dollar token on a secondary market
b) Redeem Dollar token for collateral worth 1 USD in the [LibUbiquityPool](https://github.com/ubiquity/ubiquity-dollar/blob/0a230f977ad91bbfb01dd28bc1d2ea77faed5237/packages/contracts/src/dollar/libraries/LibUbiquityPool.sol)

On early project stage any large swap may affect the Dollar token price greatly and the pool (where the swap occurred) may remain unbalanced for a long time which in turn depegs the Dollar token.

As a part of this issue we should create an arbitrage bot (i.e. `nodejs` app) which could be run on VPS or any suitable PAAS (heroku, cloudflare, etc...) to catch arbitrage opportunities in order to keep the Dollar token USD pegged on early project stage.

What should be done:
1. Create a new `nodejs` app that will catch arbitrage opportunities for the Dollar token
2. Add unit tests for basic functionality
3. Prepare a clear README of how to run the bot

Notes:
- It makes sense to create the arbitrage bot in a separate repository.
- Deployed contract addresses (mainnet): [here](https://github.com/ubiquity/ubiquity-dollar/blob/0a230f977ad91bbfb01dd28bc1d2ea77faed5237/packages/contracts/broadcast/Deploy001_Diamond_Dollar_Governance.s.sol/1/run-latest.json)

title: Test ubiquity-os
Enable JavaScript inputs in the JSX lint recipe
body:
## Summary
The lint recipe tells readers to add `.jsx` files to `include` and to set a JSX compiler option, but the illustrated lint TSConfig enables neither `allowJs` nor `checkJs`. TypeScript excludes `.jsx` from a project without JavaScript support, so the prescribed ESLint `parserOptions.project` configuration reports that the files are not part of the lint program instead of checking them.

## Trigger
Apply the recipe to a target containing `.jsx` files and run the described ESLint configuration; it errors that the lint TSConfig does not include those files.

## Evidence (source-only)
- `.agents/skills/ubiquity-code-style/references/deno.md:145-152` instructs adding `.tsx`/`.jsx` extensions and a JSX compiler option only.
- The TSConfig block above it (`:130-142`) sets neither `allowJs` nor `checkJs`.

## Acceptance
- The recipe adds `allowJs: true` (and the required JSX option) to the lint-only program when covering JSX.
- The equivalent guidance in the canonical style reference is updated, and a JSX target lints without the not-included error.

## Files
- .agents/skills/ubiquity-code-style/references/deno.md

title: Automatic Transfer
body:
The permit generation plugin should also optionally be able to automatically invoke a transfer to the beneficiaries. 

This introduces additional complexities because it must be able to estimate the gas fee of the transaction (given that we must support multiple EVM networks, with varying levels of activity, it is not viable to hard code this.)

In an org/repo config we can have a property related to payments `transfer: true`

It should also allow for the kernel operator (@ubiquity) to take a fee[^1^]. This fee should be configured elsewhere, perhaps in Cloudflare Worker Secrets (partner projects should not be able to change this.) Any fees that we take should be direct transfers of Ubiquity Dollars to `ubq.eth`.

[^1^]: This means we have to start thinking about how to capture value from payments moving around in our system. I think that we need to make a superior developer experience with our SDK and permit requests, so that plugin developers can easily capture value from the transactions their plugins are helping with.

title: Automating Call To Action Delivery (Repo XP Report)
body:
We envision that on our upcoming landing page for the XP product, we need to have a call to action that will convince users to pay for the product. 

The idea is to have them input a repository URL and then we can send them an XP report of the last month for their team. Ideally this would be in the form of a link to the dashboard so they can see everything. 

I imagine that we can leverage the tech from https://github.com/0x4007/travel-stipend/ to trigger a run using text-conversation-rewards https://github.com/ubiquity-os-marketplace/text-conversation-rewards/actions/workflows/compute.yml @gentlementlegen please add any necessary details like what branch its on and how to make this all work together. 

### Details on running `text-conversation-rewards` action

- we need to run this securely either through the kernel or calling directly by providing the proper signature
- there should be a way to know if that was previously run on this repo to avoid running it multiple times
- we can ignore private repositories
- at the end of the run, we can send the results via email to the user
- XP is based on priority / rewards combination, we need a way to define what the labels would have been, theoretically

### Safety

We must only allow this to work once per organization. This is so they can only get this free report one time. In theory this can be circumvented if they transfer repos to new orgs but that seems like a lot of headache and unlikely for established orgs to do.

title: Nomic Embeddings Model for +10% Accuracy
body:
The vector embedding model that we use is slightly outdated. I did some research to see what has higher accuracy, and I found one with 10% increased accuracy. We should make use of it as well as our old model.

## Leaderboard

Model | Top-5 Retrieval Accuracy (%) | Notes
-- | -- | --
Nomic Embed v1.5 | ~86.2% | Highest overall retrieval accuracy in semantic search benchmarks, especially strong on short & direct queries. Open source and highly accurate.
Voyage-3-large | ~75-77% | Best model from Voyage AI, state-of-the-art in industry, notably outperforms OpenAI text-embedding-3-large by ~9.7%. Strong on domain-specific tasks.

## Tradeoff

> When you submit a GitHub comment that exceeds the token capacity of the embedding model, typically:
> - The model will truncate the input at its token limit (e.g., 8,192 tokens for Nomic or 32,000 tokens for Voyage).
> - This means any text beyond the max token limit is ignored, which can lead to loss of context and reduced embedding quality if important content is cut off.

## Solution

> 2. Similarity Functions
> - Key Point: Embeddings from different models generally cannot be directly compared using the same similarity function (e.g., cosine or dot product) unless their vector spaces are aligned.
> - Each model produces numerical vectors in its own latent space, meaning the scale, direction, and semantic meaning may differ dramatically.
> - Comparing Nomic vectors against Voyage vectors directly will yield misleading results.
>
> What To Do:
> - In practice, keep embeddings from each model in separate indices or collections.
> - For each query or search, use the correct index according to the embedding model used: maintain “Nomic space” and “Voyage space” separately.

## Remarks

GitHub comment limit is 65,536 characters ≈ 16,384 tokens (rough estimate.) This means that especially comments with metadata unlikely will be able to rely on Nomic (8,192 max tokens)

## Research

https://www.perplexity.ai/search/best-vector-embeddings-model-CSpgO23jTBW5AHrh30a0cA

title: Implement Differential Reward Distribution for Reopened Issues
body:
When an issue is reopened and closed again, the reward system should calculate and distribute only the difference between previously granted rewards and new rewards.

**Requirements**:
1. Track Previous Rewards
   - Store transaction history with amounts per beneficiary
   - Record payment mode (direct/permit) used for each distribution

2. Differential Calculation
   - Compare new reward amounts with previously distributed amounts
   - Calculate positive differences only (additional rewards)
   - Skip beneficiaries with no change in rewards

3. Distribution Logic
   - Only process transactions for beneficiaries with positive reward differences
   - Handle cases where original payment failed but issue was reopened

4. Error Handling
   - Validate transaction history before processing
   - Handle missing or incomplete previous distribution data
   - Log detailed comparison between old and new reward amounts

**Technical Considerations**:
- Must not conflict with wallet insolvency fallback (generates permits if wallet can't afford payouts)
- Extend Supabase schema to track complete distribution history
- Implement comparison logic in `payment-module.ts`
- Update GitHub comment format to show differential amounts

**Example Scenario**:
```typescript
// Original distribution
{
  "user1": { total: 100, paid: true },
  "user2": { total: 50, paid: true }
}

// New calculation
{
  "user1": { total: 150, difference: 50 },
  "user2": { total: 50, difference: 0 },
  "user3": { total: 25, difference: 25 }
}
```

**Success Criteria**:
- Only processes payments for positive differences
- Provides clear audit trail of all distributions
- Handles edge cases: failed payments, partial distributions should never happen with the insolvency fallback.
- Handle what happens if we change the mode (direct, permits only) between distributions

body:
## Premade Configurations vs. Default Plugin Manifests

We aim to streamline the experience for pilot partners by providing **premade configurations**. This approach reduces the need for partners to manually configure plugins. In addition, we provide two alternative ways to modify configurations:

1. Utilize [this feature request](https://github.com/ubiquity-os/plugins-wishlist/issues/65).
2. Contact customer support for manual adjustments.

### Default Plugin Behavior

1. When a plugin uses `defaults` that are **not** sourced from a **premade config**, it retrieves its configuration from the plugin's `manifest.json` in its respective repository.
2. These defaults originate from `pluginInputs.ts` and are used across multiple infrastructure components, including:
   - This UI
   - Natural language configuration edits
   - Plugin schema and input validation (kernel-side)
   - Other relevant subsystems

#### Opinionated Defaults

There is a general concern about **opinionated defaults**. Instead of enforcing such defaults, we should **only share premade configs with partners**, eliminating the need for them to define their own configurations.

Reference: [Discussion on opinionated defaults](https://github.com/ubiquity-os-marketplace/command-start-stop/pull/151#discussion_r1991092437)

### Configuration Modes

Currently, there are three configuration modes:

- **Minimal**
- **Full Defaults**
- **Custom**

These modes, up to this point, have not been enforced to be unopinionated. Some configurations are highly opinionated and may not align with the principle of **non-opinionated defaults**.

---

## Proposed Solutions

### 1. Establish a Collection of Premade Configurations
- Define a structured set of **premade configs**.
- Ensure each premade config abstracts its functionality at a high level.
- Reduce the cognitive load on partners.

### 2. YAML-Based Template Structure
To further simplify configuration management, I suggest we use a **YAML template** with the following structure:

```yaml
metadata:
  name: "UbiquityOS Standard Config"
  description: "The fully-enabled and battle-tested configuration which we use across all organizations at Ubiquity."
  version: "1.0"

plugins: ...
```

This template includes:
- **Metadata**: Describes the premade configuration.
- **Plugins**: Lists installed plugins with relevant settings.

This abstraction ensures partners **"don’t have to think about it."**

---

## Handling Plugin Expansion

### Default Non-Expanded Behavior
@gentlementlegen [suggests](https://github.com/ubiquity-os/ubiquity-os-plugin-installer/issues/40#issuecomment-2670919061) that plugins should be installed in a **non-expanded state**. This means:

- **Infra fetches only the non-opinionated defaults** when retrieving the plugin’s manifest.
- **If plugin details are expanded**, infra should fetch its specific config **before** relying on the manifest.

### Supporting Only Premade Configs
If we only allow **premade configs** and restrict editing to **already installed plugins**, then:

- Each `premade` configuration will be expanded by default.
- This ensures we avoid relying on **non-opinionated defaults**, which may not align with intended user experiences.

---

## Conclusion

- **Premade configurations** should be the standard approach.
- A **YAML-based template** simplifies configuration abstraction.
- **Non-expanded installations** should default to non-opinionated configurations.
- **Expanded plugin configurations** should fetch predefined configurations before falling back to defaults.

By enforcing these principles, we create a **streamlined, user-friendly**, and **low-maintenance** approach to plugin configuration management.

title: admin:models tasks classify loopback by URL prefix instead of the parsed hostname
body:
**What is wrong:** `deno task admin:models` and `deno task admin:models:spark` decide whether a `BASE_URL` is loopback with the shell patterns `http://localhost*|http://127.*|http://[::1]*` (`deno.json:19-20`). Those are case-sensitive prefixes, not hostname checks: `http://localhost.example.com` and `http://127.0.0.1.example.com` are treated as loopback and queried with no credential requirement, while valid local endpoints such as `http://LOCALHOST:8000` or the expanded IPv6 loopback `http://[0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1]:8000` are rejected as non-loopback. The `:spark` variant then pipes the response through `jq`, so a remote 401 leaves it with an empty list and exit status 0 — a silent "no models" result instead of the intended credential error.

**Where:** https://github.com/ubiquity/ai.ubq.fi/blob/5c58eca89b88d7e4004521ece5350e5bebb76c1b/deno.json#L19 and https://github.com/ubiquity/ai.ubq.fi/blob/5c58eca89b88d7e4004521ece5350e5bebb76c1b/deno.json#L20. The server classifies a parsed hostname instead: `src/auth/local-admin.ts:28-48` normalizes case and brackets and accepts `localhost`, `::1`, `0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1` and the `127.0.0.0/8` range.

**Current proof:** present at development `5c58eca89b88d7e4004521ece5350e5bebb76c1b`; both task definitions are unchanged from validation head `dfcb82280f8c3236811cd3384f9bb1ac9a618ee9`. Source read only — no task, build, or runtime was executed for this validation. Originally reported from the PR #227 review.

**Trigger:** export neither token variable, then run `BASE_URL=http://localhost.example.com deno task admin:models` (no error) or `BASE_URL=http://LOCALHOST:8000 deno task admin:models` (spurious credential error).

**Acceptance:** parse the URL hostname once and classify it the same way the server does (case-insensitive, bracketed IPv6, `127.0.0.0/8`, `::1`), rejecting a non-loopback host without a token; a focused shell/Deno check covers `localhost.example.com`, `LOCALHOST`, and expanded IPv6 loopback. Keep the loopback defaults unchanged.

title: Narration decision record keeps unsupported statistical conclusions
body:
The 2026-09-21 narration entries in `docs/DECISIONS.md` still assert conclusions their own data do not support, and the correction entries repeat the same errors. The record is the repository's decision authority, so the surviving claims can steer future work.

## What is wrong
- Cross-route control: the model-versus-gateway conclusion rests on a comparison whose cells do not traverse the same gateway path (DeepSeek goes through its translation route while `gpt-reserve` does not), so it cannot clear the gateway for the DeepSeek route as written ("A translation or transport defect in this gateway would not spare one provider and hit the other on an identical body", `:675`).
- Pooled rate arithmetic: the six DeepSeek bands above 1k narrate 3+4+1+5+4+5 = 22 of 60 runs = 36.7%, recorded as "pooling to 38%" (`:678`, table `:658-667`).
- Effort conclusion: "reasoning effort is ruled out as the cause" (`:697`) is stronger than the measurement (only `gpt-reserve` was swept at medium and max; the DeepSeek sweep is underpowered at n = 10 per cell), and the same entry records 20-60% variation across DeepSeek tiers (`:654-667`).
- Falsification headline: the correction entry headlines "That is falsified" (`:589`) while its own time-controlled contrast is non-significant (`p = 0.47` each, `:615`), so context length is not excluded as a trigger.
- Window mismatch: the artifact correction compares full-session totals against the handoff's explicitly windowed observation (2026-09-21 13:26-13:56 UTC, handoff `:50`) and then concludes the measurement "cannot be reconstructed" (`:550-562`).
- Classifier mismatch: the artifact correction uses as counterexamples messages "followed by a tool call" (`:565`), while promise-narration is defined in the handoff as a trailing message with "no tool call after it" (handoff `:57-58`), so those examples are negatives under the recorded classifier.

## Acceptance
- The record either corrects each claim or narrows it to what the cited measurement supports: same-path control, 36.7% (37%) pooling, the effort conclusion limited to the matched max comparison and marked underpowered, falsification language replaced with "unconfirmed", counts compared inside the stated window, and the documented classifier applied before concluding the original count was an artifact.
- Historical 2026-09-21 entries may keep their original numbers, but each carries an explicit superseded/qualified annotation rather than being silently rewritten.

title: Terminal-mapping handoff contradicts its own G1/G2/G3 rules
body:
`docs/handoff/gateway-terminal-truthfulness-handoff-2026-09-21.md` contradicts itself between its research summary, its G1 stop-reason table, and its G2/G3 decision rules. The document is still cited as the program's specification, so a reader can implement the wrong terminal mapping.

## What is wrong
- G2 evaluates "at least one tool call" and then "a non-empty assistant message" before the stop reason (`:310-318`), so a `length` stop that already produced output matches the first rows and is reported as `completed`, defeating G1's `length` row (`:284-292`).
- G1 maps `stop` "(or absent)" to `response.completed` as unchanged behavior (`:288`), directly contradicting the research summary two sections earlier: "never treat an absent reason as proof of a normal stop" (`:257-260`).
- G3's trigger is "answer-bearing output is empty and no tool call was emitted" (`:344-345`), which is exactly the reasoning-only case, so it competes with G1's `length` mapping and with the Cerebras reasoning-only policy in `AGENTS.md:67-70`.

## Acceptance
- The document orders terminal validity after the stop-reason mapping, or states the precedence explicitly.
- An absent reason is treated as unknown/fail-closed rather than as a normal stop.
- G3 is scoped to zero output items so reasoning-only outcomes stay with G1/G2.

Source confirmation at development 1d7e64e6b30cef212bca16ca7191f13685382ded: [handoff :257-260, :284-292, :310-318, :344-345](https://github.com/ubiquity/ai.ubq.fi/blob/1d7e64e6b30cef212bca16ca7191f13685382ded/docs/handoff/gateway-terminal-truthfulness-handoff-2026-09-21.md#L257-L260), [AGENTS.md:67-70](https://github.com/ubiquity/ai.ubq.fi/blob/1d7e64e6b30cef212bca16ca7191f13685382ded/AGENTS.md#L67-L70).

title: Allow safe verification retry for an installed VPS release
body:
An interrupted public health check can fail the VPS deployment after the immutable candidate is installed, selected and restarted. Retrying `deno task deploy:vps` for that unchanged revision then rejects the existing release before either acceptance check, so the deployment cannot complete its own verification without manual recovery.

Acceptance:
- Provide a bounded safe verification retry for the already installed and selected candidate without overwriting its immutable release or adding a product flag.
- Preserve the deployment lock, checkout validation, exact release identity checks, failure status, and retention only after successful verification; reject incompatible or untrusted existing release state.
- Add a synthetic regression where public verification fails after candidate installation and a second invocation verifies that same candidate after the fault clears. Preserve fail-closed behavior while the fault remains.

Source validation:
- Static review at merged `development` SHA `5c58eca89b88d7e4004521ece5350e5bebb76c1b`; no deployment, service operation or test was executed.
- `ops/deploy.ts:169-173` installs and selects the candidate; `:182` restarts it; `:205` awaits the single public check, whose `:57` fetch has a five-second deadline.
- A public-check failure exits through `finally`, which only closes the deployment lock (`:216-218`). The next same-SHA invocation throws at `:155-158` before reaching ingress reload or health verification.
- The deployment file is byte-identical to the reviewed head: both Git blobs are `9f68d620815e3603ccc6896407cf16a504fdf11e`.
- `ops/README.md:47-54` documents manual restart and rollback. These are recovery workarounds, so this is a P2 / `Priority: 2 (Medium)` follow-up, not a claim that a transient public-check failure always leaves an outage. Suggested existing estimate: `Time: <2 Hours`.

title: Cold OpenRouter catalogue refresh delays unrelated model requests and ignores the enabled selection
body:
When the OpenRouter catalogue snapshot is cold and an API key is configured, `resolveOpenRouterUpstreamModel` awaits a catalogue fetch for any requested model id, and the Responses path awaits it before checking whether OpenRouter is enabled at all. Every coalesced request after a restart can therefore pay the catalogue timeout (now 20 s) even when the id cannot be served by OpenRouter.
## What is wrong
- `resolveOpenRouterUpstreamModel` returns early only when a snapshot is already warm or no key exists; otherwise it awaits `fetchOpenRouterModels()` and re-resolves (`src/provider/openrouter.ts:66-72`). It never rejects a non-OpenRouter-shaped id before the refresh, and the id shape is only checked by the post-refresh lookup (`openRouterUpstreamModelFor`, `:52-55`).
- The catalogue transport timeout is `OPENROUTER_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS = 20_000` (`src/provider/openrouter.ts:22`), so the stall is up to 20 s.
- Chat path: the provider-enabled check now comes first, but with OpenRouter enabled a non-OpenRouter id (default or explicit Codex model) still awaits the cold refresh (`src/chat/envelope.ts:578`).
- Responses path: the await happens before the enabled check (`src/responses-handler.ts:806`), so even a disabled OpenRouter with a configured key still contacts the catalogue on a cold cache.
## Current evidence
- `src/provider/openrouter.ts:22`, `:52-55`, `:66-72`.
- `src/chat/envelope.ts:578`.
- `src/responses-handler.ts:806`.
- Codex reviews: discussion_r4151411427 and discussion_r4151411430 on PR #567 head 9b5dc6fa26ae; both files unchanged since that merge.
## Reproduction
- Static only: cold snapshot plus key present, request a Codex id, and follow both paths to the awaited refresh. Optional dynamic proof belongs to a registered host run, not this analysis.
## Acceptance criteria
- Ids that cannot be OpenRouter-shaped skip the cold refresh, and the provider-selection check precedes any refresh on the Responses path.
- Focused tests cover a cold snapshot with a Codex id and with OpenRouter disabled.
## Duplicate search
- Snapshot search for both finding ids and for `cold catalogue`/`cold refresh`: no issue. PR #567 is the source only.

Current upstream rechecked: `1d7e64e6b30cef212bca16ca7191f13685382ded` (`development`). The affected implementation files are unchanged from the validator's `98ccd167cca1db4309e2d7f4d961b7109b119502` snapshot.

title: Fail an Ultra refusal over when the requested model id is spelled with different case
body:
## Problem

The dispatch table normalizes model ids case-insensitively — `lithosUpstreamModelFor` compares `model.trim().toLowerCase()`, so `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-ULTRA` is accepted and dispatched to the canonical Ultra model. The failover ladder does not: `lithosFailoverLadderFor(modelRaw)` is an exact-case `Map` lookup (`src/provider/lithos-rate-limits.ts:21-32`), and its callers pass the client's raw spelling (`src/provider/lithos-handlers.ts:394`, `:523-525`). A differently-cased accepted id therefore has an empty ladder, and a 429 on it is never load-balanced onto the healthy `-fast` tier.

This was originally reported by a native Codex review of PR #501 ([P2] Canonicalize the model before looking up its sibling, original cite `src/provider/lithos-rate-limits.ts:241`); the review predicted the replacement ladder lookup would retain the case-sensitive behavior, and it does at `development` `1d7e64e6b30cef212bca16ca7191f13685382ded`.

## Acceptance

- The ladder, ladder-target check, and sticky-window lookups resolve the canonical id that dispatch already accepts.
- A focused fixture proves a differently-cased Ultra id fails over to `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-fast` on 429.

## Files

- `src/provider/lithos-rate-limits.ts:21-63` — ladder and window lookups
- `src/provider/lithos-handlers.ts:394`, `:523-525` — callers
- `src/provider/lithos.ts:263-272` — the case-insensitive resolution they must match

title: Callbacks - event handlers and hybrid plugins
body:
I want to improve the experience of setting up event handlers and hybrid plugins.
I imagine something like this

```js
.on("issue_comment.created", "action", handler1)
.on("issue.closed", "worker", handler2)
```

The SDK would handle calling the Action or run it normally as a Worker and in case you're running it locally it would execute Action handlers locally too. 
Sometimes the reason why we need to call it as an Action is because some libraries are not supported by CF Workers so it'd be also good to have an option to run it as an Action even if you're running it locally.
Current hybrid plugins use `ACTION_REF` to know which Action to call but it'd be great if we could somehow get it automatically but I realize that may be not feasible.

At this point I would also consider merging `createActionsPlugin` and `createPlugin` for seamless experience.

I also realized that maybe we don't need kernel credentials to trigger Action from the Worker but only a fine-grained Github token that would only have access to the repo. Because we don't change the payload but only forward it to the Action, we don't need to generate a new signature and we can keep the original.

title: Honor no-transform and strip modern digest headers when rewriting HTML
body:
The HTML revision decorator rewrites responses that upstream marked `Cache-Control: no-transform` (request or response directive), and it leaves modern `Content-Digest` and `Repr-Digest` headers intact, so rewritten HTML is delivered with hashes of the original representation.

Priority: P2 (Codex review severity, both findings).
Native review evidence: review `router` (ubq.fi-router) on vps, cwd `/home/codex/repos/ubiquity/ubq.fi-router`, reviewed base `91bebfb78f2b`, reviewed head `06748e4f494d2d8c815d4441c8f6e4d0f3dbca6e`, exit 0, session `01a0c9b3-f37e-7a41-8d70-05802d1070d2`.

Scenario, finding 1: a successful, unencoded HTML response carries `Cache-Control: no-transform`. The predicate still permits decoration, so `proxyRoute` modifies the payload despite the upstream's explicit requirement for byte-preserving delivery. The request directive has the same problem.

Scenario, finding 2: upstream HTML includes `Content-Digest` or `Repr-Digest`. The current removal list strips only legacy digest fields, so these survive; integrity-verifying clients reject the response because the hashes no longer match the modified body.

Acceptance:

- Decoration is skipped whenever the request or the response `Cache-Control` contains `no-transform`.
- Both modern digest headers are removed alongside the existing validators on any rewritten response, in addition to the legacy fields.
- Regression coverage includes no-transform in the request, no-transform in the response, and `Content-Digest`/`Repr-Digest` removal.

Files:

- `src/utils/revision-footer.ts:52-58` — digest header removal list

title: Preserve token selector holdings and amount labels across inventory refreshes
body:
The token selector rebuilds from a symbol-keyed inventory cache and from partial core-token refreshes, which merges same-symbol contracts, drops still-owned tokens, resets selection, and leaves the amount label showing the previous token after selection is restored.

Priority: P2 (Codex review severity, all three findings).
Native review evidence: review `uusd` (uusd.ubq.fi) on vps, cwd `/home/codex/repos/ubiquity/uusd.ubq.fi`, reviewed base `eb0386e074f1`, reviewed head `9463ed2cb48647e6b4dcb69d5256e1c489896fb8`, exit 0, session `01a0c9b3-f40b-7640-86d0-2a95b7eacb2d`.

Scenario, finding 1: a wallet holds two contracts with the same symbol. `InventoryBarComponent._handleRefreshData()` merges them by symbol and overwrites one holding. Switching the selector to that cache removes an address that the previous address-based iteration over `RefreshData.tokenBalances` retained, and because the preloaded group is hidden the lost token cannot be selected again.

Scenario, finding 2: after a successful trade, `_handleTransactionSuccess()` calls `inventoryBar.refreshBalances()`. `_loadBalances()` fetches only LUSD, UUSD, and UBQ and replaces the entire inventory cache. Rebuilding from that cache drops still-owned tokens such as USDC whenever an eligible core holding remains, resets their selection, and prevents another trade with them until the next successful centralized refresh.

Scenario, finding 3: a refresh makes the selected deposit token ineligible. The amount is labeled using the old selection before `_renderTokenOptions()` switches to LUSD. The balance subscription then auto-populates and quotes LUSD while the input still reads, for example, `Amount (UBQ)`, and neither auto-population nor `_renderOutput()` corrects the label.

Acceptance:

- The inventory cache is address-keyed before the selector relies on it, so same-symbol contracts remain distinct and nonzero holdings stay selectable, per `docs/DECISIONS.md:11`.
- Partial core-token refreshes preserve the complete wallet snapshot, keeping still-owned tokens selectable and their selection intact, per `docs/DECISIONS.md:13`.
- The amount label is computed after the options and selected address are restored, so it always matches the active token.

Files:

- `src/components/simplified-exchange-component.ts:177-179` — symbol-keyed selector source
- `src/components/simplified-exchange-component.ts:184-190` — partial refresh replacing the cache
- `src/components/simplified-exchange-component.ts:758-762` — amount label ordering

Related: uusd.ubq.fi#62 is open and partially overlaps. Its scope covers keeping nonzero wallet tokens selectable when pricing is missing and rendering selector entries from merged inventory balances, which maps to findings 1 and 2; finding 3 (amount label after selection restore) is not covered. This issue records the concrete same-symbol collision, partial-refresh loss, and stale-label regressions on the reviewed candidate.

## Overview  
Enable seamless wallet connectivity in the dApp by integrating the Reown platform's AppKit toolkit, supporting wallet login, transaction approvals, and cross-chain interactions. This spec is focused on Ethereum-compatible chains using `WagmiAdapter`. The solution uses React/Next.js as the UI framework.

## Goals  
- Support secure wallet connections without exposing private keys  
- Provide users wallet management (login/logout, transaction signing)  
- Utilize Reown's AppKit for enhanced UX, security, and multi-chain support  

## Tools and Libraries  
- `@reown/appkit/react` - Core UI and functionality kit  
- `@reown/appkit-adapter-wagmi` - Adapter for Ethereum EVM chains  
- `wagmi` - Ethereum hooks for React wallet management  
- `@tanstack/react-query` - Data caching and syncing (used by AppKit)  

## Setup Steps

### 1. Project Initialization  
- Use Reown’s CLI to bootstrap your AppKit integration:  
```bash
npx @reown/appkit-cli
```
- Select your project name, framework (React or Next.js), and network library (`wagmi` recommended for EVM).  
- Enter project folder and install dependencies:  
```bash
cd your-project-name
npm install
```

### 2. Register Your Project on Reown Cloud  
- Create a free account at [[cloud.reown.com](https://cloud.reown.com/)](https://cloud.reown.com)  
- Create a new AppKit project; obtain the **Project ID** for configuration  

### 3. Environment Configuration  
- Create a `.env` file at the root of your repo, add:  
```env
NEXT_PUBLIC_PROJECT_ID=your-reown-project-id
```

### 4. AppKit Setup in Code  
- Create a config file (e.g., `config/index.tsx`) to set up AppKit with WagmiAdapter and chains:  
```tsx
'use client';

import { createAppKit } from '@reown/appkit/react';
import { WagmiAdapter } from '@reown/appkit-adapter-wagmi';
import { mainnet, arbitrum } from '@reown/appkit/networks';

const wagmiAdapter = new WagmiAdapter({
  projectId: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_PROJECT_ID!,
  networks: [mainnet, arbitrum],
});

export const appKit = createAppKit({
  adapters: [wagmiAdapter],
  networks: [mainnet, arbitrum],
  projectId: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_PROJECT_ID!,
  metadata: {
    name: 'Your DApp Name',
    description: 'Description of your dApp',
    url: 'https://your-dapp-url.com',
    icons: ['https://your-dapp-url.com/icon.png'],
  },
  features: {
    analytics: true, // optional
  },
});
```

```tsx

```

### 6. UI Integration and Wallet Connect Button  
- Use hooks like `useAppKitAccount()` to query wallet connection state and provide connection UI  
- Build wallet connect/logout buttons in your UI, styled with Chakra UI components for consistency  
- Example minimal connect button snippet:  
```tsx
import { useAppKitAccount, useAppKitModal } from '@reown/appkit/react';
import { Button } from '@chakra-ui/react';

function WalletConnectButton() {

- Test wallet connections on supported networks (e.g., Ethereum mainnet, Gnosis)

title: Cow Swap Cash Out
body:
I was doing some research on [implementing automated cowswap orders](https://github.com/0x4007/travel-stipend/blob/feat/auto-swap/src/cowswap-swap.ts) (they have an SDK) and I realize that we can do something pretty cool:

1. Only support settlements using UUSD. 
2. Allow the user to configure what asset they want to be paid in, it should be saved in localStorage. 
3. The cowswap quote can appear in place of the reward amount. For example, by default, loading the app for `100 UUSD` permit would show that. But if the user configured to get paid in USDT, then it might come out to something like `99.5 USDT`. The app will simply display `99.5 USDT` instead if their settings are set as such. 
4. The claim permit button would actually 1. invalidate their permit (if the wallet can afford the pay out) 2. initiate a cowswap order with the beneficiary address set to the permit beneficiary

Then now we can enforce people using UUSD in the backend but user facing they can receive rewards in any asset they want! 

I think this provides best of all worlds for users. For partners, we could charge a premium for them to use other tokens natively in the background etc.

I was experimenting with allowing codex to plan sprints (post all the GitHub Issues with correct labels, parent/child issue relationships, and blocking/blocked by relationships) using the below prompt.

It works quite well and I think there is value to build this out as a capability for our manager.

---

## GitHub Issues & Sprints

This project manages work via GitHub issues and sub‑issues. Keep specs concise and avoid redundancy.

### Hard Rules

- Do not create or apply sprint labels. Do not apply pricing labels.
- Do not prefix titles with sprint codes (e.g., `[S1]`). Titles must be plain and descriptive.
- Do not add tasklists to parent issues; sub‑issues in the UI are the source of truth.
- Use real newlines in bodies (never literal `\n`).

### Minimal Spec Format (child issues)

- Title: descriptive (e.g., `Sorting: clickable headers with asc/desc`).
- Labels: apply exactly one time label (e.g., `Time: <2 Hours`) and one priority label (e.g., `Priority: 3 (High)`).
- Body:
  - First paragraph: one or two sentences describing the change.
  - `Acceptance:` section with short bullet criteria.
  - `Files:` section with bullet list of paths (optionally with starting line), e.g., `- src/web/app.ts:1`.

### Sprint Parent Issues

- Keep the body to the sprint spec only. No tasklists. No title prefixes.
- Link children using sub‑issues only (UI shows them automatically).

### Parent↔Child Linking (Sub‑issues)

- Use REST `sub_issues` endpoints (underscore). The child must be referenced by its REST numeric `id`.

List children:

```
gh api /repos/<REPO>/issues/<PARENT_NUMBER>/sub_issues -q .[].number
```

Add child:

```
child_num=16
rest_id=$(gh api /repos/<REPO>/issues/$child_num -q .id)
gh api -X POST -H "Accept: application/vnd.github+json" \
  /repos/<REPO>/issues/<PARENT_NUMBER>/sub_issues \
  -F sub_issue_id=$rest_id
```

Verify parent of a child:

```
gh api /repos/<REPO>/issues/<CHILD_NUMBER> -q .parent_issue_url
```

### Dependencies (optional)

- If needed, use REST `blocked_by` to express dependencies. Avoid tasklists for dependencies.

### Issue Dependencies (blocked_by / blocking)

Preferred: GraphQL API (works reliably on github.com). Use these standalone prompts (copy/paste) — no external files.

- Add “blocked by” using GraphQL `addBlockedBy`:
```
REPO=<OWNER/REPO>; TARGET=<issue number>; BLOCKER=<issue number>
issue_id=$(gh issue view -R "$REPO" $TARGET --json id -q .id)
blocker_id=$(gh issue view -R "$REPO" $BLOCKER --json id -q .id)
gh api graphql -f query="mutation { addBlockedBy(input: { issueId: \"$issue_id\", blockingIssueId: \"$blocker_id\" }) { issue { number title } blockingIssue { number title } } }"
```

- Remove “blocked by” using GraphQL `removeBlockedBy`:
```
REPO=<OWNER/REPO>; TARGET=<issue number>; BLOCKER=<issue number>
issue_id=$(gh issue view -R "$REPO" $TARGET --json id -q .id)
blocker_id=$(gh issue view -R "$REPO" $BLOCKER --json id -q .id)
gh api graphql -f query="mutation { removeBlockedBy(input: { issueId: \"$issue_id\", blockingIssueId: \"$blocker_id\" }) { issue { number title } } }"
```

- Read dependencies via GraphQL:
```
OWNER=<OWNER>; NAME=<REPO_NAME>; N=<issue number>
gh api graphql -f query="query { repository(owner: \"$OWNER\", name: \"$NAME\") { issue(number: $N) { blockedBy(first: 20) { nodes { number title } } blocking(first: 20) { nodes { number title } } } } }"
```

Notes
- REST endpoints for issue dependencies exist in docs, but may return 404 depending on token type/feature rollout. Prefer GraphQL for portability.

### Label Policy

- Do not create custom labels; read existing labels and choose from them.
- Allowed: exactly one time label (`Time: …`) and one priority label (`Priority: …`) per child issue.
- Disallowed: sprint labels, price labels, and ad‑hoc custom labels unless explicitly requested.
- Parents (sprint umbrella issues): do not set any time label to avoid double counting.

### Time Estimate Policy (Aggressive Defaults)

- Docs and small copy: `Time: <15 Minutes` (use LLM-assisted drafting and quick edits).
- Minor UI wiring (single header behavior, simple handler, or small filter): `Time: <1 Hour`.
- Moderate client work (URL state, drill-through, saved views, CSV export): `Time: <2 Hours`.
- Heavier but contained UI work (print stylesheet, lightweight charts, design tokens, a11y/keyboard, simple virtualization): `Time: <4 Hours`.
- Re-evaluate if scope expands; prefer aggressive estimates by default and adjust upward only with justification in the issue body.

title: Pass transport factories to viem's fallback
body:
## Summary
`dynamicRpcTransport` calls each transport with its parameters before handing the results to viem's `fallback`, so the array contains initialized transport results rather than transport factories. viem invokes each entry as a function while building the fallback client, which throws before any request is sent.

## Trigger
Run the app with differing primary and fallback RPC URLs (the default production `/rpc` plus public fallbacks); pool reads and public-client creation fail with `TypeError: fn is not a function`.

## Evidence (source-only)
- `src/wallet/config.ts:52-63` maps the transports with `next(params)` and passes the mapped results to `fallback(...)`, then returns a request function.
- The locked viem 2.x `fallback` implementation calls every supplied entry as a transport factory when the client is constructed.

## Acceptance
- The fallback receives unevaluated transport functions (for example `[primary, ...rest]` without the `map`).
- A test covers a two-endpoint chain where the fallback entry is exercised.

## Files
- src/wallet/config.ts (dynamicRpcTransport)

title: Resolve the selected RPC when each request is made
body:
## Summary
The runtime-selected RPC base URL is read inside the transport factory that viem calls once per client, and wagmi memoizes that client. Because the app renders before the health probe finishes, an already-created client keeps its original endpoint after the probe selects a fallback and continues hitting the slow or wrong-chain primary.

## Trigger
Load the app with a failing primary RPC; after the probe resolves a fallback, the wallet client still requests the original endpoint.

## Evidence (source-only)
- `src/wallet/config.ts:52-63` calls `createTransport()` (which reads `getResolvedRpcBaseUrl()`) inside the factory that builds the transport config.
- `src/wallet/config.ts:67-72` builds the transport map once at module scope.

## Acceptance
- The selected RPC is resolved inside the request handler (or the cached client is invalidated when the selection changes).
- A test switches the selected endpoint after client creation and observes the next request on the new endpoint.

## Files
- src/wallet/config.ts (dynamicRpcTransport)
- src/utils/rpc-runtime.ts (selection)

title: Apply the health-check deadline to response decoding
body:
## Summary
The health check races only receipt of the response headers against its deadline. For a supported injected fetcher that ignores abort and returns headers but never finishes the body, the await on `response.json()` can hang forever, so the health check and the runtime initializer never move to the next candidate.

## Trigger
Use an injected fetcher that resolves with headers and a never-ending body; the health probe remains pending past its deadline.

## Evidence (source-only)
- `src/utils/rpc-health.ts:73-86` races `fetcher(...)` with the deadline and stores the resolved response.
- `src/utils/rpc-health.ts:92` then awaits `response.json()` outside that race.

## Acceptance
- The complete fetch-and-decode operation is raced against the deadline.
- A test with a headers-only never-ending body resolves as a timeout and tries the next candidate.

## Files
- src/utils/rpc-health.ts

title: Dismiss reverted-receipt toasts when the status clears
body:
## Summary
A reverted transaction reported on the success channel creates a persistent error toast. The bridge dismisses that toast only when the success message changes, so clearing the status (which happens before every staking action and on wallet changes) leaves the stale revert visible while the channel is empty and the next transaction is pending.

## Trigger
Trigger a reverted transaction, then start another staking action so the status channel is cleared; the previous revert toast remains.

## Evidence (source-only)
- `src/ui/toast/StatusToastBridge.tsx:58-77` returns early when `successMessage` is null and does not dismiss `failureToastId`.
- `src/ui/toast/StatusToastBridge.tsx:74-77` creates the persistent failure toast for failure-outcome messages arriving on the success channel.

## Acceptance
- Clearing the success channel dismisses a toast that was tracked from it.
- A test covers revert, clear, and next pending action with no stale toast.

## Files
- src/ui/toast/StatusToastBridge.tsx

# Error Handling & Status Toasts – Handoff

Objective
- Implement consistent error/success handling and user feedback via lightweight toasts/snackbars across key flows (RPC read failures, approve/stake actions, reward claim), without introducing large UI kits.

  - Network/RPC errors (query layer) → show succinct error with retry guidance.

- Clear, non‑noisy toasts appear for simulated failures (e.g., forced RPC error) and success flows.

title: Keep the catalog failure notice visible during proposal edits
body:
After a catalog fetch failure, the still-installed suggestion listener removes the recovery notice on the next proposal edit, leaving a disabled repository selector and issue link without any explanation.

Priority: P3 (Codex review severity).
Native review evidence: review `org` (ubiquity/.github proposal composer) on vps, cwd `/home/codex/repos/ubiquity/.github`, reviewed base `12609d2488f2`, reviewed head `b314c3ba466faa19c4caf791a463e58192f065ec`, exit 0, session `01a0c9b4-c1f4-7523-9479-8a13cb3988ad`.

Scenario: `loadRepositories()` fails, displays recovery instructions, and returns an empty array, but the proposal-edit listener remains installed. The next proposal edit calls `renderSuggestions()` with no results, which removes the failure notice. The user is left with a disabled repository selector and issue link and no indication of what went wrong or how to recover.

Acceptance:

- While the catalog is unavailable, proposal edits do not render suggestions or clear the failure notice.
- Recovery instructions remain visible until a retry or reload succeeds.
- Regression coverage simulates a failed catalog fetch followed by a proposal edit and asserts the notice is still present.

Files:

- `proposal-router/main.js:128` — proposal-edit listener that clears the notice

Related: ubiquity/.github#123 is the open parent feature request; this is a separate small recovery-path defect from the P2 issue on the same unpushed revision.

title: Preserve explicit repository choice and title edits in the proposal router
body:
The proposal router forgets an explicit repository confirmation when the user re-picks the already auto-selected value, and it can overwrite a custom title typed while the catalog request is still in flight.

Priority: P2 (Codex review severity, both findings).
Native review evidence: review `org` (ubiquity/.github proposal composer) on vps, cwd `/home/codex/repos/ubiquity/.github`, reviewed base `12609d2488f2`, reviewed head `b314c3ba466faa19c4caf791a463e58192f065ec`, exit 0, session `01a0c9b4-c1f4-7523-9479-8a13cb3988ad`.

Scenario, finding 1: the user opens the repository dropdown and chooses the already auto-selected repository. The native select emits no `change` event, so `explicitSelectionKey` stays null. Explicitly choosing the displayed payment repository and then changing the proposal text toward kernel/webhook topics silently retargets the issue to the kernel repository, breaking the promised preservation of explicit choices.

Scenario, finding 2: the catalog request is slow. The visible title field remains editable while execution is suspended before its input listener is registered. A custom title entered during that interval is not recorded as manual, and the initial `updateSuggestions()` overwrites it with `inferTitle(proposal)`.

Acceptance:

- Choosing the currently displayed repository records an explicit selection that later inference cannot override.
- Manual-title tracking is registered before the first await, or the field is disabled until initialization finishes, so a typed title survives catalog loading.
- Regression coverage exercises both the re-pick path and a title typed during a delayed catalog fetch.

Files:

- `proposal-router/main.js:10` — title listener registration after the catalog await
- `proposal-router/main.js:133-135` — explicit selection tracking

Related: ubiquity/.github#123 is the open parent feature request for the proposal router; implementing PRs #132, #133, and #134 are closed. It does not track these defects.

@ubiquityos we need to fix the cash out interface on pay.ubq.fi because its currently not vertically center aligned.
